title: Notification Lead Time Timeline
placeholder: Click either reminder for a sample message and why it goes out when it does. Click Event Day for what the two-touch pattern actually buys.

items.label: First reminder
items.hint: Day −14 — gives families time to plan
detail: This is the reminder that changes what a family does. Two weeks is long enough to move a shift, arrange a lift, or say no early enough that you can offer the place to somebody else.
"Coding Club showcase is on Tuesday 14 March, 4–6pm, in the library. Families welcome. Reply if you can come so we know numbers."
Date, time, place, and what is being asked of the reader. A reminder without an ask is an announcement.

items.label: Second reminder
detail: This one does not change plans, it prevents forgetting — so it should be short and carry only what somebody needs in the next 24 hours.
"Reminder: showcase tomorrow, 4pm, library. Bring your project if you'd like to show it."
Too late to arrange anything, and it lands while people are already committed elsewhere. The day before is the last point at which a reminder is still actionable.

items.label: Event day
items.hint: What two touches buy over one
detail: Two reminders, doing two different jobs. The first buys planning time; the second prevents forgetting. A single reminder can only do one of those.
Both, differently. Only the 14-day one and people plan to come and forget. Only the day-before one and people remember but cannot rearrange.
A third reminder does not add a third job — it repeats one of the first two, and it is the point at which recipients start filtering the club's mail. Two touches, two purposes, stop.
This cadence is a sensible default, not a measured result for your club. Track replies against reminders for a term and you will know your own numbers.
